name: Micro-SaaS
blurb: A small subscription software product for a narrow niche, run by one person or a tiny team
title: Micro SaaS Ideas: How It Works, What It Takes and the Risks
description: What a micro-SaaS is, how small SaaS products make money, what you need to build one, who it suits, the real risks and how to validate SaaS ideas before coding.
answer: A micro-SaaS is a small software-as-a-service product that solves one specific problem for a narrow group of users, such as a booking add-on for one e-commerce platform, and charges a monthly or yearly subscription. One person or a tiny team can run it. The catch is that building is the easy part: finding customers, handling support and keeping up with the platforms you depend on take most of the time, and many products never reach enough paying users.

body: Customers pay a recurring subscription, usually in tiers by usage or features, and sometimes an annual plan at a discount. Some products sell through an app marketplace (a store, accounting or website platform), which brings users but takes a commission and sets the rules.

Costs are mostly hosting, third-party services, payment fees, marketplace commissions and your time on support. The quiet margin killer is churn: customers who cancel each month have to be replaced before revenue can grow.

ul: Programming skill, or a no-code stack you know well, plus basic hosting, backups and security habits.
A narrow, painful problem you have seen first-hand, ideally in a niche that is too small for big software companies to bother with.
A way to reach that niche: a community, a marketplace listing, content or direct outreach.
Payments and subscription billing through a payment provider, with sales tax or VAT on digital services handled as your customers' countries require.
Terms of service, a privacy policy and data-protection basics (for example the GDPR if you have EU users).
Months of evenings or weekends, since early growth is usually slow.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: Developers who also enjoy talking to users
People who only want to code and never sell
Someone with insider knowledge of a niche
Anyone needing steady income within weeks
Patient builders who can support a product for years
Those who drop projects when they stop being new

ul: Building before validating: the most common failure is a finished product nobody asked for.
Platform risk: if you live inside one marketplace or API, a policy, fee or feature change can end the business.
Churn and support load: small customers cancel often and still expect fast answers.
Copycats: a narrow idea that works is easy to clone; your edge is service, niche knowledge and distribution.
Idea lists and boilerplate sellers: buying a list of "profitable SaaS ideas" or a starter kit does not give you customers.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Write down the problem in the users' own words, taken from forums, reviews or interviews.
Talk to ten potential users and ask how they solve it today and what that costs them.
Put up a landing page with a price and an early-access or pre-order button.
Solve the problem manually or with a spreadsheet for two or three users first.
Only start building once a few people have paid or committed in writing.
Define the one core feature and leave everything else out.
Build and launch it to your early users, with billing working from the start.
Set up error tracking, backups and a simple support inbox.
Track sign-ups, conversions to paid and cancellations every week.
Ask every cancelling customer why they left.
Spend at least as much time on finding users as on new features.

faq.q: How is micro-SaaS different from a regular startup?
faq.a: A micro-SaaS aims to be small, focused and usually self-funded, run by one person or a few. A venture-backed startup aims for fast, large growth and raises money to get there.

faq.q: Can I build a micro-SaaS without coding?
faq.a: Yes, some founders use no-code tools, especially for internal-style tools and simple workflows. You may hit limits on performance, cost or customisation as you grow.

faq.q: Where do good micro-SaaS ideas come from?
faq.a: Usually from repetitive problems you have seen in a job or hobby, complaints in niche forums, and gaps in popular platforms' app marketplaces. Validate before you build, whatever the source.
